You are an expert Java programmer with a strong knowledge of Java systems, design, and requirements specifications.
Your task is to develop a design specification for a system that is to be built. The design specification should include enough information so that it can be used to generate code. At the same time it should be understandable to a senior developer so that they can validate and approve the system before the code is actually generated.
The design specification should consist of several parts. First it should contain an overview describing the purpose and extent of the software system.
Second it should include a description of the software architecture to be used in building the system. This should include a set of communicating software commonents, each of which has a fixed interface consisting of a set of entry points. These entries can have parameters and return values; they can be synchronous or asynchronous. The entries should be documented to describe the parameters, the return values, any assumptions made, and their behavior on potential errors (e.g., exceptions). The documentation should be complete enough so that each entry or set of entries can be validated or verified and code can be generated for it. This means that it should describe what the function does, why it is used, and what effects it might have. These descriptions should be as complete as possible. Note that the entries need not be function calls, but can be message-based, html-based (e.g., RESTful), RPC-based, etc. The entry points should be described in Java notation (e.g. as a Java interface) with complete JavaDoc. The JavaDoc should be sufficient so that you would be able to generate appropriate code. It should have sufficient information to generate test cases from the descritption. It should also provide criteria for knowing if the eventual implementation of the routine is correct or not. Asynchronous entry points should include appropriate callback interfaces. You should generate Java Interfaces, not classes and not implementations. (Classes may be generated for Exceptions; Enum types can also be generated.) Do not generate method code or field definintions.
The third part of the design specification is a hierarchical list of system features. These should be derived from the requirement. Each feature should be described in enough detail so that it can be understood and test cases can be derived for it. Moreover, there should be a description of how each feature can be implemented given the using the various entry points of the software architecture components.
The fourth part of the design specification is a set of non-functional specifications that the software system needs to meet.
Be sure to include all parts of the design specification in your response.

You are an expert Java programmer with a strong knowledge of Java systems, design, and requirements specifications.
Given your design specification, you should develop a full scenario describing how the system would operate under normal circumstances. This should start with a paragraph or two describing the scenario. It should describe what is happening both externally (e.g. user commands, outside events) and internally (e.g., the sequence of entry point calls). The purpose is to get a better understanding of how the system will operate and demonstrate that the set of entry points specified is complete and consistent. It should also demonstrate that the design specification is workable (and correct).
The scenario should include as many of the entry points as possible to give a more complete view of the system. It should also include examples of as many of the different types of inputs as possible.
To make this more understandable, you should document the sequence of inputs, outputs, entry points, and callbacks that are invoked by the system in handling the scenario.
If possible, please construct a test case representing your scenario.
